turns.prompt_text: I wish to build a youtube media compiler. The problem I am facing is that I have to spend too much time on youtube to get any of the valuable information I need to solve problems. I have many channels that I can only learn from in aggregate, so I need to pay attention for a long time, months of a video every now and then really before I fully understand the context of what they are speaking about. The narrative, the community, the references. I really don't have all the time and energy in the world, however I would like to build some kind of net, and some automated digestor to consume the video content. I understand that some topics and channels may not be good for this as their content may be highly visual, I think that we could eventually break those down in the future. For now I believe that Youtube channels and videos that use captions and are primarily language-based work just fine. The issue I have now is in finding a good scraper tool, because scrapers are a paid subscription service, I want to try a few of them and compare results before I continue. Some youtube videos do not have captions, some have poor captions, I need to build a process it seems to get the most high-quality data. This system must be able to give some quality estimate on each video. For now we are focusing primarily on captions to keep it very light. We could easily move to audio, but the beast I wish to stay away from for now is video. I think downloading the full video for local processing would be required for that intensity of data recognition. Referencing other material would also be helpful. Information is not isolated, when in aggregate, a layer of context information about the playlist or channel may be aggregated for post-processing the videos. The context information makes understanding the references and nuances much simpler.
turns.response_html:
Building an automated YouTube digestor is a massive time-saver. YouTube is dense with information, but it's often buried under hours of pacing, narrative framing, and inside-community references.

Since you are looking to pull this data into a local context net and bypass the heavy compute of video processing, you need a pipeline that handles three things: extraction, a "quality gate" to filter out garbage captions, and a lightweight audio fallback for when captions fail.

Here is how you can structure that pipeline, especially if you are wiring up the multi-agent execution loop in Rust.

1. The Extraction Layer

You do not need paid SaaS scrapers for this. The open-source tooling for YouTube is exceptionally robust, provided you use the right libraries.

  • youtube-transcript-api: This is the gold standard for text-only extraction. It is a Python library, but you can easily spawn it as a child process from your Rust backend or wrap it in a lightweight local REST API. It fetches transcripts directly from YouTube's internal endpoints without needing a headless browser.
  • yt-dlp: If you need more than just the text, yt-dlp is the ultimate command-line tool. You can configure it to download manually created subtitles (--write-sub), auto-generated subtitles (--write-auto-sub), and crucially, video metadata and comments, which you will need for your context net.

2. The Quality Gate

Before you pass a transcript to an LLM or agent to digest, the system needs to evaluate if the text is actually usable. You can build a lightweight quality estimator using a few heuristics:

  1. Track Type: youtube-transcript-api flags whether a transcript is manually created or auto-generated (asr). Manual tracks get an automatic pass.
  2. Punctuation Density: Auto-generated YouTube captions famously strip out periods, commas, and capitalization. You can write a fast script to check the ratio of punctuation marks to total words. If it falls below a certain threshold, the transcript is likely a raw, unformatted text wall that will confuse an LLM.
  3. Word Rate: Calculate the total words divided by the video duration. If the words-per-minute is unusually low, it might be a highly visual video (like a silent coding tutorial or hardware teardown) that text alone won't capture.

3. The Audio Fallback (Avoiding Video)

When a video has no captions, or the quality gate flags the auto-generated captions as unusable, you do not need to download the video. Video files are massive and slow to process.

Instead, use yt-dlp to extract only the audio track (e.g., -x --audio-format mp3). You can then pass this audio file to a local Whisper model. If you are keeping things in Rust, whisper.cpp has excellent Rust bindings. It runs extremely fast on local hardware and will generate a clean, accurately punctuated transcript that you can feed back into your digestor pipeline.

4. The Context Net

Information isn't isolated. To understand the community and the references, your agent needs context beyond the transcript itself.

When processing a video, pull the channel description, the playlist it belongs to, and the top 20 comments. Comments are vital—they often contain community inside jokes, corrections to the video, and timestamps that highlight the most valuable parts of the runtime.

By aggregating this metadata alongside the cleaned transcript, you can map the outputs directly into local markdown files.

Formatting the digested output with standard frontmatter (tags, channel name, references) allows you to dump the results straight into an Obsidian vault. Over time, as your agents process more videos from the same channels, the hypergraph will naturally connect the recurring community references and narratives without you having to watch hundreds of hours of footage.

turns.prompt_text: So I've tried this before using the YouTube Downloader command line tool I think I have not tried the YouTube transcript API. The problem I run into is when I am downloading a vast quantity of videos, like an entire channel, which could be 300 or many more videos. I'm okay with doing this over a longer time if that's necessary. But I would also like to forecast how long it will take. Because I have so many videos I would like to analyze, the problem is making too many API calls and getting ip banned.
turns.response_html:
Running into HTTP 429 ("Too Many Requests") errors or IP blocks is the rite of passage for any YouTube scraping project. YouTube's anti-bot infrastructure doesn't care if you're pulling 4K video or just 50 kilobytes of text; if your request pattern looks robotic, they will drop the hammer.

Since you are willing to let this run over a longer period, you have a massive advantage. You can trade speed for stealth. Here is how you configure your tools to act like a human and forecast exactly how long your pipeline will take.

1. Beating the 429 (IP Ban Prevention)

To safely scrape a channel of 300+ videos, you need to introduce "jitter" (randomized delays) and manage your session state so YouTube sees you as a human casually browsing, not a server ripping data.

  • Randomized Sleep Intervals: Never pull videos back-to-back. If you are using the youtube-transcript-api in Python (or Rust via bindings), introduce a randomized delay between requests. A delay of 3 to 8 seconds between transcripts is usually enough to fly under the radar. In yt-dlp, you can do this natively with the --min-sleep-interval 5 and --max-sleep-interval 15 flags.
  • Throttle Download Speeds: When you do need to fallback to audio extraction with yt-dlp, do not max out your bandwidth. YouTube monitors the speed at which connections consume data. Use --limit-rate 500K to throttle the download speed.
  • Cookie Injection: YouTube often throws a sign-in or consent prompt that breaks headless scrapers. You can bypass this by passing cookies from a real browser session (e.g., yt-dlp --cookies-from-browser firefox). Warning: Use a burner Google account for this, not your primary Gmail. If YouTube decides to ban the account making the requests, you don't want to lose your personal data.
  • Chunking: Do not request 300 videos in a single loop. Process them in batches of 40 to 50, then enforce a long "cooldown" sleep of 15 to 30 minutes before starting the next batch.

2. Forecasting Your Pipeline

Because you are building a system that selectively decides between fast text (captions) and slow data (audio), your timeline will depend on the channel's caption quality.

Here is how to calculate the forecast for a 300-video channel:

Scenario A: The "Perfect" Channel (100% Transcripts) If every video has usable captions, you completely bypass the download phase.

  • Execution time: ~1 second per API call.
  • Random sleep: ~5 seconds per call.
  • Total per video: 6 seconds.
  • Total for 300 videos: 1,800 seconds (30 minutes).

Scenario B: The "Worst-Case" Channel (100% Audio Fallback) If the quality gate fails every transcript, you must download the audio for local Whisper processing. Assuming an average video length of 15 minutes (~20MB of audio at standard compression).

  • Throttled download (-r 500K): ~40 seconds per video.
  • Random sleep: ~10 seconds.
  • Whisper.cpp processing (on decent local hardware): ~15 seconds per video.
  • Total per video: 65 seconds.
  • Total for 300 videos: 19,500 seconds (~5.5 hours).

In reality, your pipeline will land somewhere in the middle. If you analyze the first 10 videos of a channel, you can extrapolate the ratio of Text-to-Audio and use that to generate an accurate ETA for the remaining 290 videos.

3. Designing for Resiliency

Because you will eventually hit a 429 error no matter how careful you are, your architecture must handle failure gracefully.

Do not build a script that starts at video #1 and stops if video #150 crashes. Build a state registry (a simple SQLite database or JSON file) that tracks the status of each video ID: pending, success, or failed_429.

If your script hits a 429, implement an exponential backoff:

  1. Catch the 429 error.
  2. Pause the entire queue for 10 minutes.
  3. Try again. If it fails, pause for 20 minutes.

With a state registry, you can stop the script on Friday, go about your weekend, and start it again on Monday, and it will pick up exactly where it left off without duplicating API calls.

turns.prompt_text: this would be really good. I just question how successful it will be because I get caught pretty easily. Anything past, or at least once I hit 25 videos
turns.response_html:
Getting blocked right around the 20 to 25 video mark is exactly where YouTube’s modern anti-bot infrastructure (specifically their SABR streaming protections and Proof of Origin tokens) drops the hammer. Simple sleep delays aren't enough anymore because YouTube is fingerprinting the session and tracking IP reputation.

If you want to scale this beyond that 25-video wall, you have to move from "polite scraping" to advanced impersonation. Here is the modern playbook for bypassing those blocks.

1. Authenticate with OAuth2 (The yt-dlp Fix)

Historically, people just passed cookies to yt-dlp. Today, YouTube frequently flags cookie-only headless sessions. The most reliable workaround is using yt-dlp's built-in OAuth2 flow.

When you use OAuth, you are generating a native device token, which YouTube trusts significantly more than a raw cookie string.

  • The Command: Add --username oauth2 --password '' to your yt-dlp command.
  • How it works: The first time it runs, yt-dlp will pause and give you a device code to enter at [google.com/device](https://google.com/device).
  • Crucial Rule: Do this with a burner Google account, not your primary one. Once authenticated, the token is saved, and you will bypass the "Sign in to confirm you're not a bot" error that usually triggers at video 20.

2. Proof of Origin (PO) Tokens

YouTube recently rolled out PO Tokens—cryptographic challenges that standard web browsers solve natively, but command-line scripts fail. If your yt-dlp is failing even with delays, it is likely because it cannot generate a valid PO token.

  • The Fix: Ensure you are on the absolute bleeding-edge nightly build of yt-dlp (it updates constantly to fight these changes). If it still fails, you may need to run a local PO Token provider (like the bgutil-ytdlp-pot-provider plugin) which uses a background headless browser solely to solve YouTube's cryptographic challenges and pass the token to yt-dlp.

3. Asymmetric Proxying (Protecting your Home IP)

If you pull 300 transcripts from a single residential IP address, you will get an HTTP 429 rate limit. However, transcripts are just kilobytes of text. You don't need a massive connection to get them.

Split your pipeline's network routing:

  • Audio Downloads (Heavy): Run yt-dlp through your standard home connection, heavily throttled, authenticated via OAuth2.
  • Transcript Extraction (Light): Route the youtube-transcript-api calls through a cheap rotating residential proxy service. Because the API calls only pull text, the bandwidth cost on a proxy is pennies. By rotating the IP every 5 requests, YouTube's rate-limiting algorithm never sees a pattern long enough to block it.

4. The IPv6 Subnet Trick

If you don't want to pay for proxies and your local ISP supports IPv6, you likely have an entire /64 subnet assigned to your router. That is quintillions of IP addresses.

  • You can configure your operating system to generate temporary IPv6 privacy extensions.
  • By passing --force-ipv6 to your scraping tools and cycling your local machine's IPv6 address every 15 videos, YouTube registers each batch as a completely different user on the network.

If you implement the OAuth2 login and split the proxy routing for the text transcripts, you should be able to leave the script running overnight to pull hundreds of videos without burning your local IP.

turns.prompt_text: With all this work, I think I'd rather just use something, some service that has already done it. I'm taking supadata, transcriptapi.com or apify. I'm going to try the free version of each of these just to demo them.
turns.response_html:
If you are hitting the 25-video wall and don't want to spend time building an anti-bot proxy network, offloading the headache to a managed API or scraper service is the smartest move. It lets you focus on building the context net and digesting the data rather than fighting YouTube's infrastructure.

Since your goal is to demo these services to see which handles a 300+ video channel best, here is a breakdown of their free tiers, pricing models, and how they handle the exact problems you are facing.

1. Supadata (supadata.ai)

Supadata is positioned as a premium, multi-platform extraction API. The major advantage here is its AI Fallback feature.

  • The Free Demo: You get 100 free credits per month on their free tier.
  • The Cost: 1 transcript = 1 credit. If a video doesn't have captions, you can tell their API to auto-generate one using AI (this costs 2 credits per minute of video). Paid plans start at $17/month for 3,000 credits.
  • Why use it: If you have videos in your 300-video queue that completely lack captions, Supadata will handle the Whisper audio-to-text pipeline for you server-side.

2. TranscriptAPI (transcriptapi.com)

This service does one thing—YouTube transcripts—and it does it through a very clean, simple REST API.

  • The Free Demo: You get 100 free credits to test the API upon signup.
  • The Cost: 1 successful request = 1 credit. Paid plans start at just $5/month for 1,000 credits. Crucially, if a request fails (e.g., the video has no captions), or if you request a transcript that is already in their cache, it costs 0 credits.
  • Why use it: It is incredibly cheap, predictable, and doesn't penalize you for querying videos that turn out to be empty. It also pulls channels and playlists natively.

3. Apify (apify.com)

Apify is slightly different; it's a cloud computing platform where developers host scraper scripts (called "Actors"). You rent the compute time to run them.

  • The Free Demo: New Apify accounts get $5 in free platform credits.
  • The Cost: Because you pay for compute, it is absurdly cheap. There is an actor literally called "YouTube Transcript API - 100% Free" (by developer omar khandji). The developer charges nothing; you only pay Apify's server cost to run it, which is fractions of a penny per video. Another actor ("YouTube Transcript Scraper") charges about $0.003 per transcript—meaning your free $5 credit covers roughly 1,600 transcripts.
  • Why use it: Apify is the best choice for brute-forcing a massive channel. Many of their actors bypass bot walls by mimicking YouTube's internal mobile APIs rather than scraping the web page, meaning they don't break or get blocked easily.

How to structure your demo

Before you commit, I recommend testing them specifically on the metadata you need for your context net:

  1. Test the Timestamps: Ensure the service returns per-line timestamps (e.g., start: 12.4, duration: 3.1), not just a massive wall of raw text. Your LLM will need these timestamps to cite its sources or link you back to the exact moment in the video.
  2. Test the Metadata: Run a test to see if the service can pull the top 20 comments, video description, and tags alongside the transcript. If a service only gives you text, you will still have to build a separate scraper for the community context.
  3. Test the Edge Case: Feed each service a video that you know only has auto-generated (ASR) captions with no punctuation, and see how clean the output is.

Since Apify gives you enough free credits to pull over a thousand videos right out of the gate, that might be the most powerful place to start for testing a full channel download.
